compareCandidate.label: Community vs. ecosystem
compareCandidate.description: A community is ONLY the living things of all species in an area. An ecosystem is the community PLUS the nonliving surroundings - water, soil, sunlight, and climate.

parts: The living part of an ecosystem

Forming the living part of an ecosystem
plainLanguageExplanation: A community is all the living things of all different species in one area, interacting together. A forest community includes every tree, bird, insect, mushroom, and microbe in the forest. Members of a community interact in many ways: some eat others, some compete for food or space, some help each other (like flowers and pollinators), and some live on or inside others. The community does not include the nonliving parts of the area - those belong to the ecosystem, which is the community plus its surroundings.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: All the different species' populations living together in one area

keyFacts.label: Includes
keyFacts.value: Plants, animals, fungi, and microbes - the living things only

keyFacts.label: Interactions
keyFacts.value: Species eat, compete, help, and live on each other

keyFacts.label: Not included
keyFacts.value: Nonliving things like rocks and water belong to the ecosystem

keyFacts.label: Example
keyFacts.value: A forest community = all its living species together

whyItMatters: Communities are the web of living interactions in any place. Understanding them explains food chains, competition, and how a change to one species can ripple through many others.
didYouKnow: A single oak tree can support a community of hundreds of other species - insects, birds, fungi, and mosses living on and around it.
